title: Perfect non-local quantum computation is impossible
authors: Marten Folkertsma, Dmitry Grinko, Gina Muuss, Florian Speelman
abstract: Non-local quantum computation (NLQC) asks two parties to apply a joint operation to their quantum inputs using an entangled resource state and one round of simultaneous quantum communication. NLQC has applications across quantum information, including attacks on quantum position verification, communication complexity, and quantum gravity.   Every bipartite unitary has an approximate NLQC protocol with finite entanglement, and exact protocols are known for several structured families. However, it has remained open whether every fixed unitary admits an exact protocol with finite-dimensional resources. We show that, even for two qubits, Haar-almost every unitary does not admit such a protocol, even when the resource state and local operations are tailored to the target.   The proof first shows that smooth deformations of an exact protocol can only change its target by local unitaries. For a fixed architecture, semialgebraic geometry limits the exact protocols to finitely many connected families, so each architecture reaches only finitely many local-unitary orbits. Taking the union over all architectures, the exactly implementable unitaries form countably many local-unitary orbits. We also show that some natural targets do not admit a protocol: the controlled phase $\mathrm{diag}(1,1,1,e^{iθ})$ has no exact protocol with finite-dimensional resources whenever $e^{iθ}$ is transcendental, for instance for $θ= 1$.   Our results also apply to localizable quantum measurements, whose outcome is obtained from local measurements on inputs and a shared entangled resource state without communication. A rank-one projective measurement in a Haar-random basis is almost surely not localizable with a finite-dimensional resource state and finitely many local outcomes.
summary: This paper proves that perfect non-local quantum computation (NLQC) is impossible for almost all target unitaries and measurements, even when using finite quantum resources. By analyzing the geometric constraints on exact protocols, the authors show that the set of achievable operations is restricted to a set of measure zero in the space of all possible operations. This result places strong theoretical bounds on quantum information processing capabilities.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether every fixed bipartite unitary or quantum measurement can be implemented exactly using a Non-local Quantum Computation (NLQC) protocol with finite-dimensional resources.
main_result: The authors prove that Haar-almost every bipartite unitary and rank-one projective measurement cannot be exactly implemented via finite-dimensional NLQC protocols. The set of exactly implementable operations is restricted to a countable union of measure-zero orbits.
method: The proof uses techniques from differential geometry and semialgebraic geometry, showing that smooth deformations of exact protocols are constrained to local-unitary transformations. This limits the set of achievable unitaries/measurements to a set of measure zero in the space of all possible operations.
model_or_system: The model is Non-local Quantum Computation (NLQC), where two parties use entanglement and communication to realize a joint unitary operation or measurement. The analysis focuses on the structure of the required quantum strategies and the resulting implemented unitary/PVM.
key_observables: The target unitary $U$ or the Positive Operator-Valued Measure (PVM) $\Phi$, and the associated isometry $F$ implementing the process.
important_parameters: Finite dimensionality of resources, the nature of the target unitary (e.g., controlled phase gate with transcendental phase), and the Haar measure on the space of unitaries.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the set of strategies forming an exact protocol is a semialgebraic set with finitely many connected components, allowing for path analysis via differentiation.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general framework for NLQC and then tackles unitaries by analyzing the constraints imposed by smooth deformations (leading to local-unitary orbits). It then extends this rigidity argument to localizable quantum measurements, showing the same measure-zero restriction.
why_interesting: This work establishes fundamental limitations on the computational power achievable through resource-constrained, non-local quantum interactions, providing deep structural insights into quantum information processing beyond simple circuit models.
